issues.legal_issue: Total failure to record prior narcotics information and communicate it to a superior officer invalidates the prosecution when no adequately explained delayed compliance occurs.
material_facts: A police officer received secret information while near a bus stand and acted on it by setting up a road blockade and searching a scooter.
The officer admitted that he did not record the information in writing or send it to a superior officer, either before or after the search.
The courts below treated the omission as excusable because recording and forwarding the information might have allowed the suspects to escape and no prejudice was shown.
A later report concerning the arrest was sent, but there was no explanation for failing to record and forward the secret information.
issues.conclusion: The requirements to record the information and communicate it to the superior officer were totally unmet. The later report and the claim that there was no prejudice did not cure the failure, so the prosecution case could not succeed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 42(1) and 42(2) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, information of the specified kind must ordinarily be recorded and a copy sent forthwith to the immediate superior before action is taken. Under the Constitution Bench decision in Karnail Singh v. State of Haryana, total non-compliance is impermissible; delayed compliance may be accepted only where the delay is satisfactorily explained, including by an urgent situation. Rajinder Singh v. State of Haryana applies that rule. Abdul Rashid Ibrahim Mansuri v. State of Gujarat and Sajan Abraham v. State of Kerala are reconciled in Karnail Singh; Sajan Abraham does not excuse total non-compliance. Substantial compliance cannot replace the statutory requirements in a case of total non-compliance. A later report under Section 57 is a separate requirement and cannot substitute for compliance with Section 42.

rule.if: narcotics_conviction_appeal and secret_information_received_before_search and information_never_recorded and superior_never_informed and not satisfactory_reason_for_delayed_compliance

predicates.narcotics_conviction_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a conviction in a prosecution involving alleged narcotics offending.
predicates.secret_information_received_before_searc: An officer received information of the relevant kind before conducting the search.
predicates.information_never_recorded: The officer did not record that information in writing at any time.
predicates.superior_never_informed: The officer did not communicate that information to the immediate superior at any time.
predicates.satisfactory_reason_for_delayed_complian: The officer gave a satisfactory explanation for delaying compliance with the recording and communication requirements.
predicates.prosecution_case_fails: The prosecution cannot sustain the conviction on the basis of the search and resulting case.

issues.definition: When a narcotics conviction appeal involves prior secret information that was never recorded or communicated to a superior, and there is no satisfactory explanation for delayed compliance, the prosecution case fails.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution fails to prove a narcotics recovery beyond reasonable doubt when the alleged presence of an official witness is substantially undermined and no independent witness was involved, in the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The prosecution claimed that an executive magistrate attended the search and recovery.
The magistrate said he travelled to the site in an official jeep driven by a particular driver.
The driver testified that the jeep logbook showed it was being used elsewhere by another official during the relevant period, and that he had not driven the magistrate to the site.
The logbook was produced and its entry was not effectively challenged; the driver’s account was not disbelieved.
The investigating officer did not involve any independent member of the public in the recovery or investigation and had not recorded any attempt to do so.
The Court considered these circumstances together with the total non-compliance with the information-recording requirements and found the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The alleged presence of the official witness was sufficiently doubtful, and the combined circumstances—including the absence of an independent witness and total non-compliance with the information requirements—meant that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove the charged case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court assessed the reliability of the recovery evidence against the ordinary-course logbook evidence, the doubtful presence of the official witness, the absence of independent witnesses, and the statutory non-compliance. It did not decide the separate arguments concerning Section 50 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.

predicates.narcotics_conviction_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a conviction in a prosecution involving alleged narcotics offending.
predicates.official_witness_presence_contradicted_b: Records maintained in the ordinary course, supported by witness testimony, contradict the claim that an official witness attended the alleged recovery.
predicates.no_independent_witness_involved: The investigating officer involved no independent member of the public in the recovery or investigation.
predicates.total_noncompliance_with_information_req: The officer neither recorded the relevant prior information nor communicated it to a superior, and the failure was not satisfactorily explained.
predicates.prosecution_not_proved_beyond_reasonable: The prosecution has not established the charged case beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.definition: Where a narcotics conviction appeal involves reliable records contradicting an official witness’s alleged presence, no independent witness, and total unexplained non-compliance with information requirements, the prosecution has not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
